section_summaries.epidemiology: Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, is endemic in the Americas, affecting an estimated 6 million people with 38,600 new infections and 10,600 deaths annually. Enzootic vector-borne transmission occurs in the southern US, and migration has spread chronic Chagas disease cases to North America, Europe, Australia, and Japan. Transmission occurs via hematophagous triatomine vectors and non-vectorially through congenital routes, blood transfusion, organ donation, and contaminated food or drink. Control efforts since the 1990s have significantly reduced incidence and prevalence in endemic areas.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Pathogenesis is influenced by parasite burden, initial infection severity, host immune response, and human genetic factors, with tissue inflammation caused directly by the parasite or secondary to the host's immune response. T. cruzi has a life cycle involving a triatomine vector and a mammalian host, where infective trypomastigotes circulate, invade cells, and differentiate into replicating amastigotes in tissues. An effective host immune response typically controls parasitemia, but tissue infection persists for life without effective treatment. Chronic Chagas disease development requires parasite persistence, involving parasite-dependent injury, immune-mediated tissue damage, and neurogenic and microvascular changes.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: The disease has an acute phase (1-2 weeks incubation, lasting 2-3 months) and a chronic phase (lifelong). Acute infection is often asymptomatic or mild, but severe cases (<1%) can involve myocarditis or meningoencephalitis, with local inflammation causing a chagoma or Romaña sign. Chronic infection can be indeterminate (asymptomatic) for years, with 20-30% progressing to clinically evident cardiac and/or gastrointestinal disease. Chagas cardiomyopathy is characterized by chronic inflammation, conduction system damage (e.g., right bundle branch block), and apical aneurysm, leading to dilated cardiomyopathy. Gastrointestinal involvement causes megaesophagus and megacolon. Congenital infection can lead to low birth weight, prematurity, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe outcomes. Immunocompromised hosts, including organ transplant recipients and HIV/AIDS patients, are at high risk for acute or reactivated T. cruzi infection, leading to severe presentations like fulminant myocarditis, inflammatory panniculitis, skin nodules, and CNS involvement.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis varies by disease phase and immune status. Acute and early congenital T. cruzi infection requires parasite demonstration in blood by microscopy, PCR, or hemoculture. Chronic infection relies on serologic tests (e.g., ELISA, IFA) to detect IgG antibodies, often requiring two different tests for accuracy. PCR is sensitive for acute/early congenital infections and monitoring in organ recipients, but mainly a research tool for chronic infection. Patient evaluation includes medical history, physical exam, family screening, HIV testing, resting 12-lead ECG, and for symptomatic or ECG-abnormal patients, echocardiography, exercise testing, 24-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring, and barium swallow/enema.
section_summaries.treatment: Only benznidazole and nifurtimox are available, requiring prolonged courses (60-90 days) with high rates of adverse effects, with benznidazole being first-line. Treatment is recommended for all acute and congenital infections, all children up to 18 years with chronic infection, and generally offered to adults aged 19-50 without advanced cardiomyopathy. For adults over 50 or those with advanced cardiomyopathy, treatment is optional or generally not offered. Both drugs are contraindicated in pregnancy or severe hepatic/renal dysfunction. Monitoring acute/early congenital/reactivated cases uses blood examination, hemoculture, and PCR; negative seroconversion is impractical for chronic infection. Cardiac management includes diuretics, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, amiodarone, anticoagulants, pacemakers/ICDs; heart transplantation is for end-stage heart failure. Digestive disease management includes diet, laxatives, and surgery for severe cases, as anti-parasitic treatment does not affect progression. Novel drugs are urgently needed.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention and control strategies involve residual application of long-lasting insecticides in human dwellings and peridomestic structures, with ongoing monitoring for re-infestation. Serologic screening of blood donors is compulsory in endemic countries, significantly reducing transmission risk. Congenital Chagas disease screening programs rely on prenatal serologic screening or IgG serology after 9 months of age for infants. Control initiatives have eliminated domestic transmission in several Latin American countries, but focal vector-borne transmission and re-infestation remain challenges.

tables.title: Specific Antiparasitic Treatment for Trypanosoma cruzi: Dosage, Regimens, and Toxicity
rows: BENZNIDAZOLE (ABARAX OR BENZNIDAZO-LAFEPE)Released in 1971 by Roche as Rochagan or Radanil but production was transferred to Lafepe in Pernambuco (Brazil) and transferred thereafter to Elea Pharma (Argentina)Approved in the United States for treatment of children 2-12 yr (Exeltis USA)Available in 100-mg tablets. Pediatric formulation in 12.5-mg dispersible tabletsStandard dosage regimen: 5-10 mg/kg/day (7.5 mg/kg/day) PO in two doses for 30-60 days in adults and children >12 years or >40 kg; 10 mg/kg/day PO in 2 doses for 30-60 days in children <12 yr or <40 kg

Dermatologic adverse effects in 25%-30%. The rash rarely progresses to exfoliative dermatitis. The dermatitis is usually mild-to-moderate and manageable with topical or low-dose systemic corticosteroids. The drug should be discontinued immediately in case of severe or exfoliative dermatitis or dermatitis associated with fever and lymphadenopathy.Gastrointestinal tract complaints in 10%-40%. Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and occasionally abdominal pain and diarrhea. (Taken with meals to minimize gastrointestinal irritation.)Dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy in 30%. Paresthesias, acute polyneuritis. It occurs most commonly late in the treatment course, and the drug should be discontinued. It is nearly always reversible but may take months to resolve.Bone marrow suppression is rare and should prompt immediate treatment interruption.Additional adverse effects include anorexia and weight loss, nausea and/or vomiting, myalgias and arthralgias, insomnia, and dysgeusia.Monitoring: laboratory testing (complete blood cell count and levels of hepatic enzymes, bilirubin, serum creatinine, and blood urea nitrogen) before beginning treatment and repeated every 2-3 weeks during the treatment course. Patients should be monitored for dermatitis beginning 10 days after initiation of treatment. Alcohol should be avoided.

NIFURTIMOX (LAMPIT)Released in 1967 by Bayer but suspended the production in Argentina in 1997. In 2000 production was resumed at the company's plant in Ilopango (El Salvador). Available in 30-mg and 120-mg tabletsStandard dosage regimen: 8-10 mg/kg/day PO in three to four doses for 90-120 days in adults; 12.5-15 mg/kg/day in three to four doses for 90-120 days in children aged 11-16 yr; 15-20 mg/kg/day PO in three to four doses for 90-120 days in children 1-10 yr

Gastrointestinal tract complaints in 30%-70%. Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and occasionally abdominal pain and diarrhea.Central nervous system toxicity. Irritability, insomnia, disorientation, and, less often, tremors. Less common but more serious are paresthesias, polyneuropathy, and peripheral neuritis. The peripheral neuropathy is dose-dependent, appears late in the treatment course, and should prompt interruption.Additional adverse effects include skin disorders, headache, dizziness or vertigo, nervous excitation, myalgias, and arthralgias.Monitoring: laboratory testing (complete blood cell count and levels of hepatic enzymes, bilirubin, serum creatinine, and blood urea nitrogen) before beginning treatment and repeated at 4-6 weeks and at the end of treatment. Patients should be weighed and monitored for symptoms and signs of peripheral neuropathy every 2 weeks, especially during the second and third months of treatment. Alcohol should be avoided.
